title: How do you decide whether a client should buy another company?
description: "Should the client buy this company?" A company buying another company (mergers and acquisitions).
hook: Acquisition cases can sound intimidating, with words like synergies and valuation. Underneath, they ask a few plain questions: is the target any good, does it fit, what is it worth, and can we make it work? Here is how to lay that out.
body:
When you will use it

A company buying another company (mergers and acquisitions).

This is a decide question: "Should we do this?" Test it against a few yes/no questions, put a number on it, and end with a clear yes or no. More on the three families of case questions.

Ask this first

Why buy: growth, capabilities, cost savings or a new market?

The structure

  • Is the target good on its own?
    • Its market
    • Its performance vs peers
    • Standalone value (cash flows (DCF) · multiples)
  • What extra is it worth to us?
    • Revenue synergies
    • Cost synergies
    • Minus integration costs
  • Can we make it work?
    • Funding the deal
    • Integration and culture
    • Regulation (competition law)
  • Is the price right?
    • Price vs value to us
    • Alternatives (other targets · build or partner)

Make it your own

Buy only if standalone value + synergies − integration costs is more than the price, and buying beats building it yourself.

The mistake to avoid

Counting synergies but forgetting integration costs, and not testing what happens if synergies fall short.

Practise with real prompts

1. Should a regional bakery chain buy a smaller rival for $60M?

Show a model structure
  • Target on its own: Its profits and growth; Value vs the $60M price
  • Synergies: Cost synergies: shared bakeries, buying, overheads; Revenue synergies: new regions, cross-selling
  • Risks: Integration, staff, customers lost; What we don't know: debts, contracts
  • Alternatives: Grow on our own; Buy a different target

Where to start: Standalone value vs price: synergies should be the bonus, not the reason.

The trap: Paying for synergies the buyer would have to deliver itself.

2. How would you value a football club for a potential buyer?

Show a model structure
  • Revenue: Media rights, match-day, commercial; Which are contracted vs at risk (relegation)
  • Costs: Player wages and transfers; Stadium, staff; net debt and squad value
  • Value methods: Multiples of recent club deals; Cash-flow value
  • Strategic premium: Brand, stadium, land; What this buyer can add

Where to start: Revenue and how safe it is: media money depends on staying in the league.

The trap: Using one method only; club deals rarely match cash-flow values.

3. Should a coffee chain buy its main coffee roaster?

Show a model structure
  • Value of the roaster: Its profits, other customers; Price vs value
  • Benefits to us: Lower cost of beans, security of supply; Quality control
  • Risks: Losing the roaster's other customers; Running a factory, a new skill
  • Alternatives: Long-term contract; Minority stake

Where to start: Alternatives: a long contract may give most of the benefit without buying.

The trap: Assuming owning it is the only way to secure supply.

Separate what the target is worth from what the buyer gains

A target business produces £5 million in sustainable annual EBITDA. At a hypothetical 7× enterprise-value multiple, its standalone enterprise value is £35 million. The buyer expects £2 million in annual cost synergies, but those benefits are not automatically worth £14 million: integration costs, execution risk, taxes and the time to realise savings matter.

If integration will cost £6 million and only half the proposed synergies can be realised, the deal may be much less attractive than the headline suggests. Also distinguish enterprise value from equity value: the latter is affected by net debt and other claims. Never compare an enterprise-value estimate directly with an equity purchase price without reconciling them.

Ask whether this buyer is uniquely positioned to earn the synergies and whether a competing bidder will demand a price that captures them. Your final recommendation should state the maximum defensible purchase price, the conditions necessary to create value and the non-acquisition alternative.
